title: Latin: The Roman Way
summary: A course in the Latin language and the civilization of ancient Rome, with guided reading, purposeful practice, and a shared journey through Roman history.
about: Latin: The Roman Way grows out of a long tradition of teaching the language in close connection with the civilization that spoke it. Its beginnings lie in First Year Latin, published in 1965 by Dr. Frank J. Groten, Jr. and John A. Anderson of The Hill School. The textbook series on which this app is based preserves much of the character of that original course while substantially revising and expanding its grammar, readings, and treatment of Roman history and culture.

The purpose of the course is to prepare students to read Latin with increasing accuracy, confidence, and independence. That requires a sound knowledge of forms and vocabulary, an understanding of how words work together, and the patience to attend closely to what a sentence actually says. It also requires something worth reading. Throughout the course, Latin sentences and connected passages introduce students to the stories, ideas, conflicts, and institutions of the Roman world.

The app extends this work by giving students more opportunities to practice and more immediate information about their progress. A student who has not yet mastered a concept can return to it in several different ways. A student who is ready to move further can find additional readings and challenges. Instructors can review the work their students have completed and adjust the expectations of the course to the needs of their classes.

The Roman road gives the course its central metaphor. As students advance through the lessons, their study of the language accompanies a journey through Roman history. Along the way, the Forum, the Circus, the Arena, and the other spaces of the app give different kinds of work a place of their own. This arrangement keeps the main sequence of instruction manageable while making further practice readily available.

The games, personae, and rewards have an educational purpose. Repeated encounters with a word or form are essential to learning it; variety can make that repetition more inviting. The Sentence Lab asks students to explain how a sentence works. The Atrium gives them opportunities to help one another understand it. Progress thus includes the habits of careful study and the willingness to contribute to the learning of others.

The Romans themselves remain the subject of serious inquiry. Their literature and history reveal a civilization that was often deeply foreign to our own, capable of extraordinary achievement and profound injustice. Students should encounter that world honestly, with enough knowledge to understand it and enough freedom to question it. I hope this course will help them discover the grandeur, beauty, and utility of Latin, and prepare them to approach its literature with both sympathy and judgment.

features.title: The Roman road
features.body: The main road connects the lessons and gives students a clear sense of where they are going. Grammatical checkpoints provide occasions to consolidate what has been learned before taking on more demanding work.

features.title: The lesson workspace
features.body: Instruction, guided notes, vocabulary, and essential exercises belong together. The lesson workspace keeps the central work of each lesson accessible without requiring students to pass through every optional activity.

features.title: The Sentence Lab
features.body: Reading Latin requires attention to relationships among words. The Sentence Lab breaks the work into manageable steps so that students can identify the structure of a sentence and support their translations with an understanding of its grammar.

features.title: Vocabulary and derivatives
features.body: Vocabulary practice gives students repeated opportunities to recognize meanings, identify forms, and recall principal parts. Cognates and derivatives connect their study of Latin with the English words they already use.

features.title: The Codex and Bibliothēca
features.body: The Codex gathers grammatical references and notes as the course develops. The Bibliothēca offers further reading, giving students occasions to use what they have learned beyond the exercises of the current lesson.

features.title: The Circus and Arena
features.body: Races and quiz contests give familiar material a different setting. The Circus encourages quick recall; the Arena provides another occasion to test accuracy and review mistakes. Both draw their educational value from the Latin practiced and the feedback that follows.

features.title: The Atrium and Forum
features.body: The Atrium gives students a place to ask questions and explain difficult material to classmates. Shared projects in the Forum connect individual progress with contributions to a larger community.

features.title: Personae and progress
features.body: Roman callings, companions, and accessories give students choices as they advance through the course. Dēnāriī provide a spendable reward, while the virtue tracks recognize different kinds of effort and contribution. These systems are intended to sustain interest over a long course of study.

features.title: The instructor’s role
features.body: Instructors can see student progress, assign work, and set expectations for further practice. The app supplies information that can help teachers decide when a student needs encouragement, a different explanation, or a greater challenge.

credits.editorHeading: Textbook series editor and app development
credits.editorBody: Editor of the textbook series; design and development of the app and its instructional activities.
credits.authors: Anderson, Groten, Lake, Ciraolo, Lake, and Turner.
credits.authorsNote: Author order follows the supplied Volume I cover. Full names and the preferred final credit line await editorial confirmation.
credits.origin: The original First Year Latin was written by Dr. Frank J. Groten, Jr. and John A. Anderson of The Hill School. The present textbook series builds upon and substantially expands their work.
technology: I have developed the app through a process of curriculum design, software development, editorial review, and classroom testing. AI tools, including ChatGPT/Codex, Claude, and Gemini, have assisted with programming, artwork, editorial work, or design planning. I direct the app’s educational design and am responsible for reviewing the material and deciding what is included.

The app continues to develop in response to classroom use. A mistaken answer key, an unclear explanation, or a technical problem can interfere with learning. Reports from students and instructors help identify such problems and guide subsequent revisions.
credits.art: The app brings together historical photographs, maps, illustrations, and artwork created for its Roman settings and personae. Historical image credits and licensing information belong with the relevant illustrations and in the photo credits. App artwork and other contributions will be identified in the final credits.

acknowledgements: My greatest debt is to the teachers and colleagues whose work made this course possible. Frank Groten and John A. Anderson established the foundation on which the textbook series rests. My co-authors and colleagues at The Hill School helped sustain and develop that work over many years.

I am grateful, too, to the students who have worked through successive versions of the text and the app. Their questions have revealed unclear explanations; their corrections have exposed mistakes; and their suggestions have helped shape the experience of using the course. The personae, companions, and races owe much to their enthusiasm and imagination.

The original textbook preface recognizes Lijun “Lucy” Lyu, Viktoria Alberts, Samuel Hunter, and Kevin Lu for their careful reading and editorial assistance. I remain grateful for their contributions. Further acknowledgements of the app’s pilot students, instructors, artists, and other contributors will be added as this work develops.
All errors that remain are my own.

feedback.heading: Help improve the course
feedback.intro: If you find an error, encounter a problem, or have an idea that would improve the course, I would like to hear about it. A useful report tells us where you were working, what happened, and what you expected to happen. If a Latin answer seems wrong, please include the sentence or question and explain your proposed correction.
feedback.boundary: For help understanding a lesson, please ask your instructor or use the Atrium. This form is for corrections, technical problems, and suggestions about the app.
feedback.privacy: Please leave out passwords, class codes, classmates’ names, and student scores. If you include a screenshot, crop it to the relevant question or problem.

labels.category: What would you like to report?
labels.details: What happened, or what would you like to change?
labels.correction: What correction do you propose, and why?

feedback.locationHelp: Include the lesson, activity, and question number when possible.
feedback.detailsHelp: For a technical problem, describe the steps that led to it. For a suggestion, explain how the change would help students or instructors.
feedback.contactHelp: An email address is needed only if you would like us to follow up.
feedback.confirmation: Thank you for helping improve Latin: The Roman Way. Your report has been received for review. Where a change is needed, it will be checked before it is added to the app.
feedback.failure: Your feedback could not be sent. Your text is still here. Please try again when the connection is available.
feedback.statusText: Reports are reviewed before any change is released. Some suggestions may require further investigation or a later stage of development.

originalPreface: This Latin textbook represents the culmination of over fifty-five years of work in the Classics Department of The Hill School, a private co-educational boarding school in Pottstown, Pennsylvania. The article to the right, from the 1965 edition of the Hill News, announces the publication of the original iteration of this Latin textbook, entitled First Year Latin, written by the Classics and Humanities Chairmen of The Hill School, Dr. Frank J. Groten, Jr. and Mr. John A. Anderson, respectively. That version of the text remained in use until sometime in the 1990s.

The revision and expansion of this text have been extensive. The organization of the original text has been considerably altered to condense it and better reflect the relative frequency and importance of certain aspects of Latin grammar, morphology, and vocabulary. The most substantial revisions, however, include the liberal use of charts, figures, maps, and illustrations and the addition of Latin readings, hundreds of original Latin sentences, and cultural and historical material—presented chronologically—that grounds the text in the full context of ancient Roman civilization. Alongside glossed and adapted Latin, the book includes sentences and passages composed for this edition. These passages use the ellipsis, ambiguity, and artful word order that make Latin literature challenging to read. In short, the text is designed to open up to students the grandeur, beauty, and utility of the Latin language so that they can make the leap to actual Latin literature as seamlessly as possible.

The text will be suitable for teachers who prefer the traditional grammar-translation method or the reading method. In addition to the use of original Latin readings (and composition) and ample cultural material, each lesson in the text features extensive drill work to help the beginning student actively master new grammatical concepts and vocabulary. Instructors may, of course, use the text in whatever way is best suited to their students’ learning styles and to the time constraints of their course. Some drill work, cultural material, or review lessons may be skipped altogether without affecting a student’s technical mastery of Latin, particularly at the college level. The original Latin sentences, while glossed, are often quite challenging and may best be read at sight in class with the instructor’s help, thus opening up natural and interesting questions about Roman literature, history, and so on.

An effort has been made to select sentences and readings that are representative of the grammatical concepts and vocabulary introduced in each Lesson and that reveal important aspects of the values, history, and culture of the ancient Romans. Much of this material may be at odds with the values that we hold today. It is important, however, for students to see and to understand the Romans as they were: deeply foreign and strange to us, often flawed, yet also profoundly influential—a civilization which has handed down to us much of the essential framework of the language, law, literature, art, architecture, and engineering of our modern world, and therefore one worthy of serious study.

All forms and vocabulary introduced in the text are located in the appendices for easy reference for the student and instructor. As the text progresses, review lessons appear more frequently to help students solidify and synthesize their understanding.

Finally, the authors would like to thank our colleagues at The Hill School for their encouragement and support. We owe our greatest debt to the original authors of the text, Frank Groten and John A. Anderson, and we hope this new text represents an improvement, while still preserving the virtues of the original. We would also like to thank our students who patiently endured earlier drafts of this textbook. Lijun “Lucy” Lyu has been especially vigilant in identifying typographical errors and other inconsistencies, and the keen eyes of Viktoria Alberts, Samuel Hunter, and Kevin Lu have also been key to the editing process. All errors that remain are my own.
